newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's ruling party signals peace on strike eve.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's ruling party signals peace on strike eve.

text.p: The chairman of South Korea's ruling party made a dramatic visit on Monday to a Seoul cathedral where union leaders are sheltering from arrest as they plot the biggest strike in the nation's history.
But plans for all-out stoppages starting on Tuesday appeared to be wavering, with hardened union activists confessing workers were losing their appetite for confrontation.
Unions had threatened the biggest ever strike on Tuesday and Wednesday over a new labour law giving employers the right to lay off workers and replace strikers.
The defence ministry said military personnel were ready to step in to keep essential services running.

Continuing a charm offensive that has stolen the thunder from militant union leaders holed up at Myongdong Cathedral, New Korea Party leader Lee Hong-koo pulled up in his limousine and sought a meeting with activists.
He was shoved aside by workers chanting "Get Out" and met instead with South Korea's Roman Catholic Cardinal.
Lee had earlier challenged leaders of the oulawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to a televised debate over the new law.

Confederation heads said they would only meet Lee if the government scrapped the law that has sparked three weeks of industrial unrest and dropped arrest warrants against them. Official figures showed production losses from strikes since the labour bill was rammed through parliament on December 26 had hit 1.96 trillion won ($2.3 billion).
President Kim Young-sam made clear the law would not be scrapped or amended.

"The stark reality facing us today is that without the labour reforms, workers will get neither the income nor jobs in the face of cut-throat global economic competition," he told ruling party lawmakers.
"I could have delayed the legislation if I had wanted to spend the final year of my term without much trouble."
Tuesday's strikes are being spearheaded by the officially recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions. It has called for a two-day walkout by it 1.2 million members.
However, by late on Monday there were signs that stoppages may have only a token impact.
Bank unions said as many as half of all tellers would show up as usual. Subway unions said that drivers would confine their protests to wearing street clothes instead of uniforms.
Stock investors were unruffled and the market finished flat, with some blue-chips even posting slight gains.
Union leaders in Ulsan, home of the giant Hyundai Group and traditional hotbed of worker militancy, admitted that sentiment was turning against industrial action.

In particular, they said workers at Hyundai Heavy Industries, the group's shipbuilding arm, were growing weary of conflict. "People are getting older and cooperation is sagging," said one union official.
The 500,000-strong confederation has urged its members to join all-out stoppages on Wednesday.
Lee's headline-grabbing visit to Myongdong cathedral appeared designed to soften the government's image. Threats to arrest union leaders have recalled the harsh methods of past authoritarian regimes.
"Lee Hong-koo's visit is a failed publicity stunt to put us in the negative light as an uncompromising radical group," said one confederation official.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung warned confederation leaders they could not evade the law forever.
Yonhap news agency quoted him as saying police would hold back from making arrests "out of respect for freedom of religion and the church's dignity", but eventually there would be a reckoning.
